title: Calling Sri Near
hookLine: Diwali night, the door left open, and a hymn that calls the goddess near and hopes she is glad to come
carry: puja: welcoming the divine as a beloved guest
tomorrow: why do coins pour from Lakshmi's hand?
last: THE ONE WHO DOES NOT GO AWAY.

cards: You hear a wedding procession before you see it. Drums from two streets over. Then horns, then a crowd, then the horse with the groom on it, swaying, decorated, a little embarrassed.
Everyone on the block comes to the window. Something important is arriving, and it's loud about it. The next line of the Sri Sukta sounds like that.
The singer hears the goddess coming before she's in the room. And when she gets there, he doesn't ask for anything yet. He asks one thing about her.

teach.b: Here's the line, in paraphrase. Horses go before her, a chariot carries her in the middle, and she delights in the trumpeting of elephants.
I call the goddess Sri near.

teach.h: MAY SHE BE PLEASED WITH ME.
teach.b: May the goddess Sri be pleased with me. Royalty arriving: Sri comes the way a queen comes into a city, and the whole street knows. Then the verb.
I call her near. The singer is still at the door, inviting. And then the request, quieter than you'd expect.
Not give me. Not bless me. May she be pleased with me.
The Sanskrit word carries the sense of taking pleasure in, being glad of. That changes the shape of the whole hymn. It isn't a vending machine, coins in and fortune out.
It's hosting someone you love and hoping they feel at home. And that is the heart of how Hindus worship.
A puja is hospitality. The deity is offered a seat, water for the feet, flowers, a lamp, food, the welcome you'd give an honored guest in your home. You can't order a guest to be happy.
You can sweep the floor, light the lamp, and hope. That's why, on Diwali night, many families leave the lamps burning and the door open: Lakshmi is being invited in. Notice the name, too.
Sri is the honor people put before other names, on a letter or a wedding card. In this hymn it's the goddess herself: radiance, beauty, good fortune, all in one word.

how: In Lakshmi worship at home, some families clean the house and light lamps before reciting the Sri Sukta, especially at Diwali, as a way of welcoming the goddess.

o: a royal parade song for a king's return home
a list of offerings that force good luck to come
a hymn hoping Sri will be glad to come and stay

p: trumpeting, and she delights in it

s: in this line, the singer demands gold from the goddess
he calls her near and asks that she be pleased with him.
Sri arrives like royalty in the hymn
horses before her, a chariot in the middle, elephants trumpeting.
in puja, the deity is treated like an honored guest
a seat, water for the feet, a lamp, food: the welcome you would give someone you love.

games.q: you're the singer. the goddess is arriving with horses, a chariot and elephants. what's the first thing you ask?
o: that she be pleased with you.
that she leave the elephants outside.
games.why: the line calls her near and asks that the goddess Sri be pleased with the singer: hosting, not ordering.

practice: Light a lamp or a candle if you can, the way families do for Lakshmi, or picture one burning by your door. Notice what a welcome would look like here: one thing straightened, one light on.
Then sit inside that welcome as if someone you love were on the way.
If you pray, you can call the goddess, or God, near in your own words and offer the light; if you don't, let the lit room be a welcome for whatever good you hope will come.

wordCard.voice: The Sri Sukta. The hymn that hears Sri coming, with horses, a chariot and elephants, and asks only that she be pleased to be here.

orig.note: Sanskrit: śrīr mā devī juṣatām, 'may the goddess Sri be pleased with me,' from the Sri Sukta.

carryVoice: Your line: puja is welcoming the divine as a beloved guest. A guest can't be ordered to be happy, only welcomed. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Sri Sukta, verse 3 (Rig Veda khila, as commonly recited)
